newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Students jeer Berisha in south Albanian town.
newsitem.headline: Students jeer Berisha in south Albanian town.

text.p: Students in southern Albania jeered President Sali Berisha on Wednesday after he rejected their demands for the government to resign and reimburse investors for money lost in a savings scandal.

The president, who must seek a fresh term of office by March 9, took time out of his schedule during a visit to Gjirokaster to meet some 700 university students who have called an indefinite boycott of classes in protest at the government's handling of failed pyramid investment schemes.
Berisha said the government bore some blame for failing to warn investors about the scams in time but the main responsibility lay with gullible investors.
"I cannot support the illegitimate request to reimburse money...(But) as a physician, I would not allow anyone to die from a hunger strike," Berisha told the students.

Students in Albania's southernmost town of Gjirokaster, near the Greek border, said on Wednesday they were boycotting classes indefinitely in solidarity with students on hunger strike in the southern town of Vlore.
Apart from Tirana, the south is the most prosperous region in Europe's poorest state and it was badly hit by the collapse of two pyramid schemes favoured by thousands of people.
The most violent clashes hit Vlore two weeks ago when one man was shot dead and two others died of heart attacks.

Speaking earlier to a rally of some 1,500 supporters at Gjirokaster's main sports hall, Berisha pledged to create a free trade zone in the area, more social assistance and credits for small businesses.
Security has been tight on Berisha's 10-day swing around the country. In Gjirokaster, uniformed police surrounded the sports hall.

In Tirana, the Forum for Democracy grouping 15 opposition parties and other groups said in a statement on Wednesday that it opposed Berisha's re-election, saying it would only deepen the crisis in the country.
Parliament elects the president and Berisha is sure to win a fresh five-year mandate with his right-wing Democrats holding 122 of 140 seats after last year's disputed general election.
The Forum also complained that police were preventing them from holding peaceful protests, a measure criticised by the U.S. State Department on Tuesday.
Plainclothes police prevented Tirana students from organising a peaceful demonstration on their own campus and threatened cameramen trying to cover the event.

State Department spokesman Glynn Davies said Washington was concerned about reported beatings of opposition members and journalists, and called on Tirana to draw up a new constitution and hold fresh elections.
But the U.S. appeal appeared to fall on deaf ears. Berisha said he had no intention of calling early elections.

"Concerning the election we have not changed our view and respect the people's verdict," Berisha told cheering supporters in Gjirokaster. "There will be no early elections. Elections will be held in 2000."
The European Union on Monday offered Albania help to get its economy and financial institutions in order, but insisted Tirana had to stick to democratic principles.
